title: Preserving evidence without tipping off the attacker
body_md:
## Preserve the trail without delaying containment

Evidence helps a bank understand a disputed payment, a provider investigate an account, and investigators connect reports. It cannot by itself make a refund or prosecution happen. For an individual facing an active takeover, removing access and reporting a live loss usually matter more than watching an attacker for a “better” screenshot. Take a quick copy when safe, then contain.

### Build a small, private case file

Record the original message or email, not only a cropped screenshot. For email, preserve the full message with headers if the mail service allows export; a displayed sender name can be forged. Save transaction references, the bank's case number, account alerts, relevant security activity, and dates with timezone. Make a timeline that separates observation (“19:10: saw transfer in bank app”) from inference (“may have started after support call”). If an entry is uncertain, mark it uncertain rather than filling the gap.

Capture the context around a screenshot so a reviewer can tell what application and date it came from; do not include passwords, recovery codes or unnecessary personal data in a shareable copy. Keep originals in a private location with a backup you control. Give a bank or investigator only the material requested through an authenticated channel. The US IC3 specifically asks complainants to retain originals securely and does not take attachments to its complaint form.

### What can disappear

Providers may rotate activity logs, messages can be deleted, and a device reset may erase local evidence. If a work device or serious malware investigation is involved, contact the response team before changing it; forensic handling is specialist work. Do not attempt to access the attacker's account, “test” suspicious links, contact the attacker, or leave them in your account to observe them. You can record an alert and then revoke sessions. Later, add confirmation letters and final outcomes to the same timeline.

widget_config.goal: Preserve a usable, private timeline and original artifacts while containing an active incident promptly.
widget_config.today_action: Create an empty incident-note template with fields for date/time/timezone, observed fact, source, action, contact and case number; store it privately.

blocks.title: The disappearing login log
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Ada finds a foreign device in her email settings and a forwarding rule. She writes down the time and captures the security page, then revokes sessions and removes the rule.
blocks.analysis: A brief record preserves context without leaving access open. She keeps the original alert and any export privately; she does not send screenshots containing recovery details to friends.

blocks.title: A legitimate bank verification request
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a bank fraud team reached through the number on a card asks Ben for a transaction reference and a copy of a receipt via its secure portal.
blocks.analysis: A real investigator may need evidence. Ben verifies the channel independently, sends only the requested receipt, and records the case number. “Never share evidence” would block a legitimate dispute.

blocks.title: An email takeover case file
blocks.setup: Synthetic: a mailbox shows an unfamiliar forwarding rule and a bank notice. You need to preserve useful evidence while stopping access.

choices.text: A short timeline, the alert and visible rule, with dates and source.
choices.consequence: You retain context before settings change.
choices.explanation: Separate what the account shows from what you suspect.

choices.text: Only a memory of what happened.
choices.consequence: Details may be forgotten or challenged.
choices.explanation: A contemporaneous record is more useful.

steps.prompt: An unfamiliar session remains active. What next?

choices.text: Keep it connected for several days to watch it.
choices.explanation: A consumer should not trade containment for speculative evidence.

choices.text: Revoke sessions through the provider and secure the account; capture later available logs.
choices.consequence: The attacker loses an access path while records remain organized.

steps.prompt: An unsolicited 'investigator' asks you to upload the full mailbox. What do you do?

choices.text: Decline and use a verified bank/provider or authority channel with only required records.
choices.consequence: You avoid exposing other people's mail and secrets.
choices.explanation: Evidence transfer must be authenticated and minimal.

choices.text: Upload everything to the supplied link.
choices.consequence: Sensitive material may go to another scammer.
choices.explanation: An unsolicited link is not an evidence channel.

steps.prompt: How do you describe a gap in the timeline?

choices.text: Mark the time as unknown and note what is confirmed.
choices.consequence: Later reviewers can distinguish fact from inference.
choices.explanation: A truthful gap is better than invented precision.

choices.text: Choose a plausible time so the report looks complete.

blocks.debrief: Keep originals and a factual timeline, contain active access, and transmit only necessary records through verified channels. Retry each decision and replay; no screenshot substitutes for stopping harm.

blocks.title: Use evidence in a different case

questions.prompt: A payment-app receipt shows a transfer. What is the most useful record?

choices.text: Receipt plus reference, time, app account and your report number.
choices.explanation: These details let the provider identify the transaction.

choices.text: Only a cropped image of the logo.
choices.explanation: It cannot reliably identify the payment.

questions.prompt: Does the US IC3 complaint form accept your evidence attachments?

choices.text: Yes, upload all files into the complaint.
choices.explanation: IC3 says it does not accept attachments.

choices.text: No; retain originals securely for an agency that may later ask.
choices.explanation: That is the IC3 FAQ's instruction.

questions.prompt: A work laptop may need forensic review. What should you do before wiping it?

choices.text: Ask the organization's response team and follow its procedure.
choices.explanation: Specialists can balance evidence with containment.

choices.text: Wipe immediately to hide the event.
choices.explanation: That can destroy evidence and violate procedure.
